facts.claim: Meta’s Llama 3 report (2024) gives its models a vocabulary of 128K pieces; the largest, 405 billion weights, was pre-trained on 15.6 trillion tokens.
Biderman and colleagues (2023) trained 16 Pythia models, 70 million to 12 billion weights, each on about 300 billion tokens over 143,000 steps, and published 154 checkpoints of every one.
Kaplan and colleagues (2020) found that a language model’s loss falls along a smooth, predictable curve (a power law) as its size, its training data and the compute spent on it grow.

Kaplan and colleagues (2020) found that growing a model without growing its data brings less and less gain on held-out text: each time the model is 8 times bigger, it needs about 5 times the data to avoid that penalty.
They concluded that the most compute-efficient training uses very large models on a relatively modest amount of data, stopped well before the loss stops falling.
Hoffmann and colleagues (2022) found that model size and training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size, double the training tokens too.
The same paper reads Kaplan’s fit as: for 10 times the compute, a model 5.5 times bigger trained on only 1.8 times the tokens.
Chinchilla, 70 billion parameters trained on 1.4 trillion tokens, used the same compute as the 280-billion-parameter Gopher and outperformed it.
Hoffmann and colleagues concluded that the large language models of 2022 were significantly undertrained: too big for the data they saw.
Lee and colleagues (2021) found that over 1% of the unprompted output of models trained on common datasets was copied word for word from the training data.
Removing duplicates let them train models that emit memorised text ten times less often, in fewer training steps.
They also found train-test overlap in over 4% of the validation sets of standard datasets.
Muennighoff and colleagues (2023) found that, with limited data, up to 4 passes over the same text gave almost the same loss as fresh text; with more repeats, extra compute eventually added nothing.
Magar and Schwartz (2022) trained models with test data mixed into pre-training and found they sometimes exploit it, scoring higher on the examples they saw than on ones they didn’t.
